overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of how phenomenological description differs from introspective psychology and from causal explanation. You'll be asked to classify sample statements, and to answer questions about why introspective psychology declined, Brentano's distinction between inner perception and inner observation, and Titchener's structuralism.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Which type of claim is this statement: "The melody seemed to rise toward a note I expected, but the note never came"?

options.html: An introspective report of elementary sensations
options.text: An introspective report of elementary sensations
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. An introspective report breaks experience into inner elements such as sensations and feelings. This statement describes the melody as it unfolded, including an expected note, so it's a phenomenological description.

options.html: A causal explanation of the hearing
options.text: A causal explanation of the hearing
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A causal explanation names physical or physiological causes, and this statement names none. It describes the melody as it unfolded, including an expected note, so it's a phenomenological description.

options.html: A phenomenological description of the hearing
options.text: A phenomenological description of the hearing
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The statement describes how the melody was given: as unfolding, and as moving toward an expected note. It's directed at the melody as experienced, not at inner sensations or causes.

options.html: A report of a physical phenomenon in Brentano's sense
options.text: A report of a physical phenomenon in Brentano's sense
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The statement describes the experience of a melody as it unfolded, including an expected note, so it's a phenomenological description.

forms.stemHtml: Why did the imageless-thought controversy damage introspective psychology?

options.html: It showed that Wundt's laboratory equipment was unreliable
options.text: It showed that Wundt's laboratory equipment was unreliable
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The controversy wasn't about equipment. Trained observers in different laboratories disagreed about their own experience, and introspection had no independent way to decide between them.

options.html: Trained observers disagreed, and introspection couldn't settle it
options.text: Trained observers disagreed, and introspection couldn't settle it
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Würzburg observers reported thoughts without images, and Titchener's observers reported faint images in similar thinking. Each side blamed the other's training, and introspection offered no independent way to decide.

options.html: It proved that thinking always involves vivid mental images
options.text: It proved that thinking always involves vivid mental images
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The controversy proved nothing of the kind. Trained observers disagreed about whether thought involves images, and introspection couldn't settle the dispute.

options.html: It showed that thinking has no conscious features at all
options.text: It showed that thinking has no conscious features at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Neither side claimed that. Trained observers disagreed about whether thought involves images, and introspection couldn't settle the dispute.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following statements are causal explanations? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: "Neural activity in the auditory cortex grouped the tones into a phrase."
options.text: "Neural activity in the auditory cortex grouped the tones into a phrase."
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This names a physiological process that produces the experience, so it's a causal explanation.

options.html: "The apple appeared as one thing, with its back side given as there."
options.text: "The apple appeared as one thing, with its back side given as there."
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. This describes how the apple was given in experience, so it's a phenomenological description, not a causal explanation.

options.html: "Low blood sugar produced the pang of hunger."
options.text: "Low blood sugar produced the pang of hunger."
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This names a physiological cause of the experience, so it's a causal explanation.

options.html: "I felt a patch of red sensation and a mild pleasant feeling."
options.text: "I felt a patch of red sensation and a mild pleasant feeling."
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. This breaks the experience into sensations and feelings, so it's an introspective report, not a causal explanation.

forms.stemHtml: What did Brentano claim about observing your own present mental states?

options.html: Present states can be observed reliably after laboratory training
options.text: Present states can be observed reliably after laboratory training
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That was closer to the introspective psychologists' hope. Brentano held that attending to a present state as an object disturbs it, so observation is possible only in memory.

options.html: Present states can be observed, but past states can never be
options.text: Present states can be observed, but past states can never be
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Brentano held the reverse. Attending to a present state as an object disturbs it, so observation is possible only in memory.

options.html: Attending to a present state disturbs it; observing works only in memory
options.text: Attending to a present state disturbs it; observing works only in memory
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Brentano distinguished inner perception, an awareness that accompanies each act, from inner observation, attending to a state as an object. He held the latter impossible for present states. His example is anger, which changes as soon as you try to observe it.

options.html: Present states can't be perceived in any way at all
options.text: Present states can't be perceived in any way at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Brentano held that we do have inner perception of present states, an awareness that accompanies each act. What we can't do is observe them, because attending to a present state disturbs it.

forms.stemHtml: What was the name of Titchener's program of analyzing consciousness into its elementary processes, the way anatomy analyzes the body?

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Titchener's structuralism asked what the mind's elements are and how they're arranged, leaving the question of what mental processes do to a separate inquiry.
Correct! Titchener's structural psychology, or structuralism, asked what the mind's elements are and how they're arranged.
Sorry, that's incorrect. Titchener contrasted his program with the study of what mental processes do. His own program was structuralism.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Titchener's program of analyzing consciousness into elementary processes was structuralism.

title: Description vs. Explanation
